text:
Andoni Iraola's Liverpool start assessed: Creating chaos, going direct and fixing leaky defence
Liverpool host arch-rivals Man Utd with new boss Andoni Iraola having been in charge for 10 top-flight games now; the Reds sit fourth having lost twice in the league; watch Liverpool vs Man Utd on Super Sunday on Sky Sports Premier League from 4pm; kick-off 4.30pm
Thursday 19 November 2026 15:12, UK
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola asked for judgements on his tenure to wait until after the November international break - we assess how the Basque is faring so far in his new role ahead of the visit of Manchester United in the Premier League on Super Sunday.
Iraola has been in charge at Anfield for less than six months after replacing Arne Slot in June following Liverpool's dismal Premier League title defence last season under the Dutchman.
The then champions could only manage an underwhelming fifth-place finish, 24 points worse off than when winning the league in 2024-25, with Slot paying with his job as a result.

Iraola was identified as the man to not only get Liverpool back to winning ways, but to also do it in a 'heavy-metal' front-footed fashion that would get fans off their seats again after what he had achieved in three hugely successful campaigns at Bournemouth.
So, 10 league games in and with Liverpool sitting in fourth place, what exactly has Iraola changed and how much progress has he made at Anfield?
Chaos over control
There has been a noticeable increase in intensity to Liverpool's game under Iraola this season, in stark contrast to the laboured displays that dogged much of the previous campaign under his predecessor.
In fact, at times Liverpool have started to resemble Jurgen Klopp's pressing monsters again, albeit with subtle differences, as Virgil van Dijk recently pointed out.
"It's a different era, different times," said the captain prior to the international break. "Under Jurgen, we pressed a lot with shuffling across, we tried to box them in one side, but football has changed.
"So, it's different - but what isn't different is the amount of sprints and running and trying to get the ball back as soon as possible.
*PPDA is a proxy for pressing intensity, it is the number of opposition passes allowed per defensive action
"You have to try to create this chaos, second balls, battles, and that's what we still are learning."
Part of that chaos Iraola has tried to create can be seen in how Liverpool's players man-mark all over the pitch on occasions with, for example, Van Dijk following his man all the way into the opposition half.
That, though, can create its own problems, according to the Dutchman: "It's a challenge because when teams know that we want to win the ball high they try to drag you into difficult spaces and you have to read the game."
That disruption can also be seen in the unpredictability of personnel in Liverpool's wide forward areas, with the Reds boss not only keeping the opposition guessing by changing who starts in those positions - regardless of which foot they favour - but by switching them in game as well.
And one of the positive knock-on effects of trying to get back to Klopp's 'heavy-metal' brand of football is it has reawakened Anfield.
Liverpool as a team have always tried to harness the power of the home fans and feed off them, especially under the German, but that was somewhat lost as a result of Slot's more prosaic, safety-first style of play.
But, according to the skipper, it is worth starting fast at Anfield to get the home faithful fully invested: "Especially here [Anfield], at the start, you have to go all in and take that risk. If you win the ball high, you see the crowd coming up as well and it just brings that energy that will help throughout the whole 90 minutes."

'Risk-reward' of going direct vs playing through the press
Part of that unpredictability under Iraola so far this season has also seen the back line - mainly Van Dijk - not be afraid to mix things up by going long to beat the opposition press, particularly at Anfield.
The stats certainly back this up, with Liverpool having been more direct this campaign [50.8 long passes per game] than either last season [46.3] or Klopp's final one [49.6], while the players are also winning more of their aerial duels in the process.
Consequently, that has meant more of Van Dijk's characteristic long-range crossfield passes out of defence looking for his pacy forwards to start attacks, although as the captain explains, it is now all about finding "the right balance' between the two approaches.
"Are you going to go direct and play the second ball or you're going to try go through them? That's the risk-reward you have to take," says Van Dijk.
"You have to be able to adapt and that's part of our jobs as well. The manager can obviously put the plan out but we as players have the responsibility in order to execute and win the game as well, with the help, of course, of the manager and the staff, but we on the pitch are the ones that have the most influence.
"We have to be a little bit more direct and that helps again winning the ball high.
"You have to find the right balance because I feel that we can still play through the press, but we can also go direct and at home sometimes you have to."
Araujo's arrival helps shore up leaky defence
One area where Liverpool have significantly improved from last season is defending set plays, a major Achilles' heel in Slot's final campaign.
Under the Dutchman, the Reds shipped a whopping 23 Premier League goals from set pieces - second only to the 26 let in by Iraola's Bournemouth - a weakness that in many ways came to symbolise their slipshod title defence.
Whereas so far this season, albeit across a much smaller sample size, Iraola's side have conceded twice from set plays, with the Basque crediting the training-ground work done by his assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper.
"I think we have, touch wood, dealt very well with defending set pieces so far this season," he said.
"It definitely helps having a centre-back [Ronalds Araujo] at right-back when we talk about defending set pieces. It helps a bit with the height and the physicality of the team."
In fact, overall since Araujo was brought into the defence at Ipswich Town in September, Liverpool have only let in three league goals with 11 men on the pitch, in stark contrast to the 53 they conceded under Slot last time out, their most ever in a 38-game Premier League campaign.
Return of Klopp's Mentality Monsters?
Last season the then champions seemed incapable of recovering from any sort of setback, as evidenced by them picking up just the five points from losing positions all season long in what was a clear sign of their waning powers of recovery and team spirit.
But already this campaign Liverpool have managed to win the same amount of points in a come-from-behind victory at Brentford, as well as draws with Newcastle United and Nottingham Forest, in a demonstration of their will to win under Iraola.
All of which will remind Liverpool fans of Klopp's 'Mentality Monsters', who were never beaten, however grave the situation, although Iraola's side still have some way to go to match the 28 points the Reds won from losing situations in the German's final season at the helm in 2023-24.
Can Iraola make Anfield a fortress again starting against United?
Bizarrely, in contrast to their unrivalled form on the road this season, Liverpool have won just once at Anfield in the Premier League, the 2-0 victory over Brighton in October, with Iraola only too aware of utilising the power of the Reds' faithful.
"At Anfield, everyone feels when the team goes for it and when everyone is giving everything and trying their best our supporters will be there to help the team," he said.
"Even when we have started losing some of the last games, they have been there and helped us massively.
"At home we have a big advantage against teams and this atmosphere we can create, this is special."
A red-hot atmosphere can be guaranteed to greet United on Sunday, especially with the visitors arriving at Anfield in the relegation zone - so what better opponents to record just a second home win in the league since April than their arch rivals from down the East Lancs Road?
